content: Changes in payment methods for healthcare providers, such as pay-for-performance (P4P) schemes, are increasingly being implemented by governments, health insurers, and employers to align financial incentives with health system goals. This review specifically examined the effects of altering payment methods and levels for healthcare providers in outpatient settings, which include care provided outside of hospitals, such as primary care. These settings are critical for reducing reliance on more expensive hospital services. The objective of this review was to evaluate how different payment methods impact the quantity and quality of healthcare services, patient outcomes, provider outcomes, service costs, and potential adverse effects. The review included 27 studies, comprising randomized trials, controlled before-and-after studies, interrupted time series, and repeated measures studies. Most of the studies involved primary care physicians and were conducted in high-income countries, with only one study from a lowor middle-income country. Key Findings: 1. Pay-for-Performance (P4P) Compared to Existing Payment Methods: P4P incentives likely improve child immunization rates (Risk Ratio [RR] 1.27, 95% Confidence Interval [CI] 1.19 to 1.36; moderate-certainty evidence). P4P may slightly increase the number of patients who are asked more detailed questions about their condition by pharmacists (Mean Difference [MD] 1.24, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.54; low-certainty evidence). P4P may slightly improve the prescribing of guideline-recommended antihypertensive medications by primary care physicians (RR 1.07, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.12; low-certainty evidence). The effects of P4P on mean blood pressure reduction and service costs are uncertain due to very low-certainty evidence. No data were reported on workload or other outcomes for healthcare professionals. One randomized trial found that the performance improvements achieved during the P4P intervention were not sustained after the intervention ended. 2. Fee-for-Service (FFS) Compared to Existing Payment Methods: The effect of FFS on the quantity of health services delivered (e.g., outpatient visits, hospitalizations), patient health outcomes, and total drug costs is uncertain due to very low-certainty evidence. The quality of service provision and health professional outcomes were not reported. One randomized trial suggested that physicians paid via FFS may see more well patients than salaried physicians (low-certainty evidence), potentially indicating the delivery of unnecessary services. 3. Mixed FFS and Existing Payment Methods Compared to Existing Payment Methods: A mixed FFS payment method may increase the quantity of health services provided (RR 1.37, 95% CI 1.07 to 1.76; low-certainty evidence). The effects of mixed FFS on the quality of services, patient health outcomes, and health professional outcomes are uncertain due to very low-certainty evidence. Cost outcomes and adverse effects were not reported. 4. Enhanced FFS Compared to Standard FFS: Enhanced FFS (higher FFS payments) likely increases child immunization rates (RR 1.25, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.48; moderate-certainty evidence). It is uncertain whether higher FFS payments lead to more primary care visits or affect net annual expenditures for covered children under regular FFS (very low-certainty evidence). The quality of service provision, patient outcomes, health professional outcomes, and adverse effects were not reported. Conclusions: P4P and increased FFS payment levels likely increase the quantity of healthcare services provided (moderate-certainty evidence). P4P may slightly improve the quality of care for targeted conditions (low-certainty evidence). The effects of payment method changes on patient health outcomes remain uncertain due to very low-certainty evidence. There is insufficient information to determine how specific design features of payment methods, such as incentive size or performance measures, influence outcomes. Evidence is limited and of very low certainty regarding whether changes in payment models without additional funding for professionals would yield similar effects. Further high-quality research is needed, particularly in lowand middle-income countries, to explore the impacts of different payment method designs and to assess unintended consequences of payment interventions.
